title: Choosing a computational model
baseline_choice: Keep linear_search as the stable correctness baseline. Offer the immutable category index for repeated queries; rebuild after catalogue updates.
measured_selection: At 10000 records, estimated category-index break-even is 1 batches of six queries (build plus query medians). None means no measured crossover. Estimates are local workload-dependent, not universal thresholds.

complexity.category_index: O(n) build and extra references; expected O(1) category lookup plus O(n_category) scan and O(k) output
complexity.one_pass_batch: Theta(n*q) comparisons worst case; one traversal does not eliminate q predicates
complexity.parallel: A redesigned filter can have O(n) work and O(log n) span; no parallel timings are claimed. Small n may be dominated by scheduling overhead.

model_choice: Use RAM costs for these resident objects; I/O models for disk/block movement, cache models for locality, and work/span for a future parallel design. Hashing helps exact category/ID lookup but does not make a price-range filter constant time.
explanation: For a small or frequently rebuilt catalogue, scan avoids index construction and extra memory. For many queries over an unchanged snapshot, amortized index build cost can be repaid. Choose from measured total workload cost, not Big O alone; Python/object overhead and fixed fixture selectivity limit generalization.
indian_context: A quant team may value predictable tail latency more than average throughput.
An HPC batch workload may justify parallel scheduling and locality-aware placement.
An Indian marketplace product team must balance query latency against stock updates, index rebuilds and memory.
timing_protocol: Warm-process calibrated batches, 7 samples in seeded shuffled order; median in microseconds. timeit disables cyclic GC. No CPU pinning/cache flushing. Parsing, profiling and tracing excluded unless explicitly named.
